Procter & Gamble vs. Colgate-Palmolive: Which Dividend Stock Is Safer?
Both consumer giants beat earnings, yet their margins are moving in opposite directions as oil prices climb and a cautious U.S. shopper holds back. One dividend carries a thin balance sheet buffer, and retirees need to know which one.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG | PG Price Prediction) and Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL) reported eight days apart, and both beat revenue and earnings expectations. For retirees, the key question is which dividend can absorb oil-driven cost spikes, currency swings, and a hesitant U.S. shopper? The two companies answered it differently.
Shoppers Buy More P&G Products While Colgate Wins on Price
P&G posted Q1 FY2027 core EPS of $2.00, beating the $1.89 estimate. Organic sales rose 4.0%, and volume supplied 2.4 points of that gain. That points to more households buying Tide and Pampers, which is the soundest kind of growth. Pampers Amore alone is projected to exceed $100 million in first-year sales. The cost is margin: core gross margin fell 150 basis points, and management sees a $1.4 billion after-tax commodity pressure that assumes $100 Brent crude. As management put it, “The strength is real, but it won’t be a straight line.”
Colgate beat with base EPS of $0.97 against a $0.93 estimate. Pricing drove 2.0% of its 3.6% organic growth, and base gross margin expanded 90 bps to 60.3%. That margin direction runs opposite to P&G’s. North America remains a soft spot, with volume down 3.7%. CEO Noel Wallace called the U.S. fix “very much a work in progress.”
Cash Coverage Exposes a Balance Sheet Gap
P&G’s forward dividend equals roughly 62% of its $7.00 core EPS guidance midpoint. That leaves comfortable room. FY2026 free cash flow of $15.84B covers the planned $10B-plus in dividends, with buybacks absorbing most of the rest.
Colgate grew free cash flow 7%, yet shareholders’ equity fell to $288M after years of repurchases. I see that thin buffer as a real constraint. Currency adds risk too: FX lifted Latin America sales by 6.5%, but Brazil’s real has since turned against the dollar.
Investors have rewarded Colgate’s margin story anyway. Its shares are up 29.3% year to date versus 21.33% for P&G.
Oil and U.S. Market Share Will Settle This in 2027
I’m watching whether P&G’s pricing-with-innovation approach holds as greater cost pressure arrives in the back half. Management wants more than 80% of its top U.S. customers holding or growing share by year-end. For Colgate, keep an eye on the 2027 U.S. innovation cycle. Wallace already warned, “We do not see the headwinds on commodities lightening up as we exit the year.”
Why P&G’s Dividend Looks Sturdier for Retirement Income
For income-focused investors considering these names, P&G offers a higher yield, a bigger recent raise, a longer run, and cash flow that covers the payout well even with core EPS guidance flat to slightly up. Colgate fits a dividend-growth investor who can stomach emerging-market currency swings for its expanding margins and Hill’s momentum. I would rethink my view if P&G cut guidance on oil, or if Colgate’s North American volume turned positive.

The survey found that 82% of finance team members at U.S. small and midsize companies would get more value from AI if their financial data were in one system.
Many businesses are expecting a leap in productivity from AI layered on top of financial systems that don't share data and lack the business context behind it. When the data underneath is scattered and stripped of meaning, AI inherits every gap, and finance teams are left to sort it out.
Scattered data and missing context leave finance teams cleaning up after AI
AI is helping finance teams work faster, but it has also shifted new work onto them. When financial data is spread across disconnected tools, someone still has to pull the information together, decide which numbers to trust, and check AI's output before it can be used. Without access to a company's financial data, policies, and accounting practices, AI also lacks the context needed to provide insights that support strategic business decisions.
Key survey findings
-
New work absorbs time savings: 81% say AI has saved them meaningful time, but 70% say it has also handed them new responsibilities without taking any existing ones away, so the time saved often goes to new work.

-
Security adds a governance layer: 66% say financial data security concerns have created additional governance and policy work around AI, rising to 74% among finance leaders.

Missouri Senate Republicans will return to Jefferson City in January with fewer seats, a flood of newcomers and new leaders who say they heard voters’ frustration Tuesday — even as they have yet to settle on what to do about it.
Sen. Jason Bean, a Republican from Holcomb chosen Thursday to serve as Senate president pro tem, said the election results made clear the party needs to reassess its approach.
“They weren’t real fond of what we’ve been doing,” Bean said of voters. “So we’re going to look at changes.”
Sen. Nick Schroer, a St. Charles County Republican selected as majority floor leader, offered a more specific diagnosis: Republicans lost because they failed to deliver on their promises, not because their agenda was too conservative.
“Voters are sick and tired of spineless politicians that promise the world and produce nothing,” Schroer said.
Democrats, meanwhile, believe the election was a rejection of the GOP’s priorities, not simply its ability to accomplish them.
“Voters are screaming that they don’t like what Republicans are doing in Jefferson City,” said Democratic Sen. Stephen Webber of Columbia, who was chosen Thursday as minority floor leader.
The competing interpretations will help shape a legislative session that begins under significantly different political circumstances.
Democrats flipped two Senate seats Tuesday, defeating Republicans in eastern Jackson County and Springfield to end the GOP’s two-thirds supermajority. Republicans will hold 22 of the chamber’s 34 seats.

The U.S. economy isn't expected to have produced much job growth in October, with employers reluctant to hire workers but also not cutting staff amid a shrinking labor force and a growing problem of long-term unemployment.
Economists are looking for a meager nonfarm payrolls gain of 59,000, a slight uptick from the 29,000 jobs produced in September, according to the Dow Jones consensus. That result would continue a pattern of sparse growth.
But that's kind of OK: The forecast also is that the unemployment rate will hold at a very low 4.2% rate, the product of a climate where a stagnant labor force reduces the need for outsized job increases to keep the jobless level steady.
"Long-term, we're not going to need as many jobs added to the economy to have stable employment because we have fewer people who are available to work," said Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at jobs site ZipRecruiter. "An aging workforce is pushing a lot of people into retirement. We have had decades of low birth rates, meaning we don't have a lot of people who are coming in to replace those retiring workers. And immigration is now down pretty significantly, which is reducing some of that prime-age employment."
Evaluating the health of the labor market in such a climate becomes a moving target, Bachaud said.
More clues will come Friday when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October nonfarm payrolls report at 8:30 a.m. ET.
"Do we have an economy where we have a lot of productivity but not as many jobs? Do we start focusing on things like wage growth? Is that more of a signal, especially for lower-wage workers?" she said. "I think that's the situation we're in right now because we're not going to go back to 200,000-plus jobs being added a month. That's just not the the scenario that that we're sitting in."

Yet the unemployment rate has barely budged, up just 0.2 percentage point despite the marked slowdown.

The 23-year-old from Easton, Pennsylvania, showed up to the starting line in Staten Island dressed as a hot dog and finished in 2:49:15, which, after hearing, made me think I could’ve done a lot more than just iron my name onto my tank top.
Pezzino, a personal trainer and group fitness coach, was attempting to break a Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon dressed as a savory food. The previous mark was 3:11:34, which, incredibly, she beat by more than 22 minutes! Guinness still has to review the evidence before anything becomes official, but judging by the number of people who noticed her on Sunday, finding witnesses won't be a problem.
When speaking with Runner’s World, Pezzino said the hot dog wasn't even originally part of her marathon plans—and neither, for a while, was running another marathon at all.
Pezzino had been competing since childhood, starting in a local running series at age 4 before moving on to cross country and track in high school and college. She made her marathon debut in Chicago in 2024. She returned the following year, but a serious medical emergency at Mile 17 forced her to drop out. A federal judge rejected Delta Air Lines’ request to dismiss a lawsuit by passengers who said they paid extra money to sit in window seats, but found themselves seated next to windowless blank walls.
US District Judge Ramon Reyes in Brooklyn ruled on Wednesday that there was a reasonable dispute over whether Delta’s contract of carriage, which says the carrier “does not offer tickets or contracts to customers that guarantee particular seats,” required Delta to provide window seats to passengers who paid for them.
Reyes did not decide the lawsuit’s merits. In July, a federal judge in San Francisco rejected United Airlines’ bid to dismiss a similar lawsuit.
Delta declined to comment on Thursday, saying it does not discuss pending litigation.
Casey Olbrantz, a lawyer for the four Delta plaintiffs, called the decision “a significant precedent in establishing that, despite federal deregulation, passengers can still hold airlines accountable when they don’t get what they paid for.”
The proposed class actions were filed in August 2025 by disgruntled passengers who found themselves seated next to walls on Boeing 737, Boeing 757 and Airbus A321 planes.
According to the plaintiffs, passengers typically buy window seats to address fear of flying and motion sickness, keep children occupied, get more light, or take in the view.
They said the absence of windows next to their seats was not disclosed during the booking process. Aircraft walls sometimes align with operating components, such as air conditioning ducts.
In seeking a dismissal of the Brooklyn case, Atlanta-based Delta said the inherent nature of airline operations, including the periodic need to substitute planes with different seating arrangements, absolved it from guaranteeing seat assignments.
Both lawsuits seek millions of dollars in damages, for more than 1 million passengers per carrier.

The United States is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” to industrial refrigeration systems, saying in a statement issued on Thursday that every organization that depends on cold storage should assume it could fall into the hackers’ crosshairs.
The statement, which follows a spate of hacks against commercial freezers in the United States and Europe, said that unidentified “malicious cyber actors” were targeting vulnerabilities in internet-accessible electronic temperature and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.

“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” said the statement, which was jointly issued by the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the departments of health, transport and agriculture.
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said Chris Butera, CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity.
FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said that the government was “seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally.”
The government urged operators of industrial refrigeration control systems to pull their devices off the public internet, isolate them from their corporate networks and promptly apply software updates.
At least three waves of hacks have hit commercial fridges and freezers in the past few months. Pentagon investigators are treating a series of mysterious malfunctions that hit grocery store refrigeration units on US military bases in August as a cyberattack, Reuters first reported last week. A sweeping hack of French freezers last month dealt tens of millions of euros’ worth of damage, while a second wave of hacking affected more than 100 stores across Europe on Monday.

Pittsburgh’s Allegheny County passed one of the nation’s most generous parental leave mandates last month, putting businesses there on the hook for as much as 12 weeks of a worker’s full salary.
After Tuesday’s elections, employers around the country have reason to pay attention.
Democratic gains in Congress and statehouses are giving new momentum to paid leave and expanded child care, issues that featured prominently in political campaigns this year. Incoming governors in Wisconsin and Georgia ran on expanding early childhood education, while voters in Marin County, California, are on track to pass a tax increase that may raise up to $12.5 million a year to help more families afford child care.
For businesses, the question isn’t just whether those policies will advance, but how they’ll work and who will pay.
Allegheny County offers a glimpse of what’s at stake. Its new rule requires companies with at least 15 employees to provide 12 weeks of parental leave at full pay after the birth, adoption, stillbirth or placement of a child, capped at $4,200 per week. Unlike state paid-leave programs that spread costs through centralized insurance systems funded by taxes on workers and businesses, Allegheny leaves employers responsible for covering the benefits themselves.
That has alarmed many Pittsburgh-area small businesses and nonprofits. Many worry they’ll have to reduce hiring or cut services in order to comply.
“Having time available for parents to spend with their kids is important for us, but the challenge was that the full burden of this policy was put on the business,” said Mark Heinbockel, the executive director of mental-health charity Anchorpoint Counseling Ministry in McCandless Township. He said his organization may have to scale back services when an employee is on parental leave.
Len Semplice, the owner of Redbeard’s Sports Bar & Grill in Pittsburgh, said he believes in parental-leave policies, especially at large companies, and is open to plans overseen by the government. He said he’s considering raising prices to preserve an already slim profit margin. “I’m going to have to charge someone to make up the difference. It goes to the consumer in a way,” he added.
He also worries people will take advantage of the policy, working the bare minimum — six months or 625 hours — to qualify for the benefit and then not return after the leave period ends. “What guarantees they’re coming back?” Semplice asked.
Nonprofits that advocated both for and against the plan estimated the policy may cost employers between $170 million to $300 million, given projections that roughly 2% of the county’s workers might use it in a given year.
The fight may already be overtaken by Tuesday’s election. Democrats won control of Pennsylvania’s state Senate, giving the party control of both chambers and the governor’s office. That may revive a statewide paid-leave policy that passed the Democrat-controlled House this year and stalled in the Republican-led Senate. The state proposal would spread the cost through a payroll deduction-funded insurance system that could supersede the Pittsburgh-area plan.

Google, Meta Platforms and TikTok sued California to block enforcement of a new state law intended to limit the risk of addicting children under age 16 to online platforms.
The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits those platforms from offering underage children “psychologically exploitative features” that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children’s accounts with those features.
In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok said the law wrongly compels them to honor the state’s preferred means of presenting content to children, and substitutes the state’s judgment for that of parents. They said the law violates the US Constitution’s First Amendment’s free speech protections, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.
Related: Snap Finalizing Settlement to Avoid LA Trial on Addiction Claims
“The state cannot, consistent with the First Amendment, override Meta’s editorial judgments about how to curate and display … billions of posts of third-party speech,” the Facebook and Instagram parent said in its complaint. Google, which owns YouTube and is a unit of Alphabet, and TikTok, a unit of China’s ByteDance, made similar arguments.
The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who enforces the state’s laws and is the only defendant, did not immediately respond on Thursday to requests for comment.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on September 10. He said children’s safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California “will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk.”
Thousands of Lawsuits Allege Addiction
Some critics accused California of overreaching by restricting children’s online access. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group, called the law “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare.”
Many U.S. states regulate children’s access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and limit teenagers’ use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all U.S. states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws.
Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in Los Angeles.
The companies and Snapchat parent Snap SNAP.N still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

Wilson said personal lines new business is up 125% over 2019, and currently split about eventually between exclusive agents, independent agents, and direct-to-consumer. However, the advent of PAAs “gives us the opportunity to serve consumers who prefer to have a machine to handle their transactions,” Wilson added.
Allstate said it does not yet have a name for its PAA, but it will leverage Allstate’s Large Language Intelligent Ecosystem (ALLIE), which is ingesting code at a much high rate than just a few months ago. Allstate said its PAA will also work with existing PAAs, such as Muse.
Related: Allstate Introduces Large Language Model, ALLIE
“Essentially, we’re now marketing to machines and people, not just marketing to people,” Wilson explained. “These capabilities also give us the opportunity to be offensive in leveraging capabilities by launching a PAA that’s an expert in protection that still meets consumers’ needs and their desires for fewer clicks.”
The PAA will additionally provide context on coverage needs of the customer, he added.
Wilson said the speed of the development of this market is unclear, but getting in now “will enable Allstate to provide increased value for customers.”
“We believe that this will actually help the existing PAAs out there,” Wilson said. When asked about possible regulatory or cyber concerns, Wilson added that Allstate will “figure out stuff like what do we do with the regulators, what do we do with privacy, what do we do with cybersecurity, as we go.”
“There’s work to be done, but the benefit to customers and the economic rationale is going to move this train down the path,” Wilson said. “This is going to happen. So we decided to get in on it, accelerate it, go as fast as we can, which is why we started leaning into the PAA.”

A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said.
The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other.
The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack.
The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said.
“Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. “So kudos to that security guard.”
The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released.
Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle.
The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees.
David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire.
People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape.
“I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.”
The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said.
Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene.
Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said.
Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage.
Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities.
Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus.
General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter.
“We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said.
Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.”
“Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said.

Voters preserved abortion rights while making it harder for lawmakers to overturn citizen-approved measures. Anti-abortion Republicans are now looking for other ways to restrict access

Missouri Republicans spent two years trying to reinstate an abortion ban. They emerged from Tuesday’s election with fewer ways to do it — and no plans to stop trying.
About 55% of voters rejected Amendment 3, preserving the constitutional right to abortion approved in 2024. Voters also approved Amendment 6, which sharply limits lawmakers’ power to overturn citizen-approved measures, while Democrats won enough legislative seats to end the GOP’s supermajority in the Missouri House.
The results dealt a significant setback to anti-abortion activists who had hoped Missouri could provide a national model for reversing abortion rights victories at the ballot box.
Missouri voters reject Amendment 3, preserving abortion rights approved in 2024
But state Sen. Nick Schroer, a St. Charles County Republican who will become Senate majority leader in January, said abortion will remain a priority for his caucus, even as lawmakers grapple with the new restrictions imposed by Amendment 6.
Schroer said the issue will be a “hot topic” at upcoming Republican caucus meetings, though lawmakers have yet to settle on a strategy. Several attorneys, including himself, are examining what options remain.
“But are we handcuffed by Amendment Six?” Schroer asked, adding that Republicans will “have to be strategic in what we do.”
Republican lawmakers placed Amendment 3 on the ballot last year, arguing that voters hadn’t understood the reproductive rights amendment they approved in 2024. But Tuesday’s results were more decisive: Roughly 55% rejected the proposed ban, compared with the 51.6% who approved abortion rights two years earlier.
“It’s hard to say this time that they were tricked,” said Matt Harris, a political scientist at Park University. “ … it’s maybe close, but Missourians have demonstrated that they want abortion rights.”

“Throughout this campaign I’ve been asked a lot about how it feels on the ground,” Mallory Schwarz, executive director of Abortion Action Missouri, said during a victory speech Tuesday evening. “The best answer I could give was people are mad, just plain pissed off that we had to do this again. Amendment 6 creates a formidable new obstacle for lawmakers hoping to revisit abortion rights through another constitutional amendment.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Crime scene tape surrounds an entry to the Barus & Holley engineering building at Brown University. The rate of violent crime victimization declined 25% between 2024 and 2025, while the rate of property crime victimization fell 19%, according to the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics’ preliminary National Crime Victimization Survey. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
A new federal report released the week before Tuesday’s midterm elections found that Americans experienced declines in several categories of violent and property crime victimization in 2025, including aggravated assaults, burglaries and motor vehicle thefts.
The preliminary survey findings from the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics offers a fresh look at crime trends as the country emerges from another election cycle, providing new data on Americans’ experiences with crime, including incidents never reported to police.
The rate of violent crime, excluding simple assault, declined 25% between 2024 and 2025, while the rate of property crime victimization fell 19%, according to the agency’s National Crime Victimization Survey.
Unlike crime statistics based solely on offenses reported to law enforcement, the National Crime Victimization Survey captures both reported and unreported crimes. The nationally representative survey interviews people aged 12 or older about their experiences with violent crime, excluding homicide, and household property crime. It also collects information about the frequency, characteristics and consequences of those incidents.
The preliminary survey results are consistent with other national crime data, including the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting program, which tracks crimes reported to law enforcement and has documented several years of declining crime rates nationwide. Preliminary FBI data suggests those declines have continued into 2026.
Independent analyses, including crime trends reports from the nonpartisan Council on Criminal Justice, have identified similar patterns, with declines reported in some of the nation’s largest cities. However, crime trends vary across communities, with some experiencing different patterns.
“To see that those things really align, it gives me much more confidence that I’ve had over these past several years that what we’re seeing is a real decline in crimes beyond homicides,” said Thaddeus Johnson, a senior fellow at the council. Johnson also is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at Georgia State University.
Violent crime declines
Americans aged 12 or older experienced an estimated 7.5 million violent victimizations in 2025, a rate of 25.7 victimizations per 1,000 people, according to the report.
The rate of violent crime excluding simple assault fell from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025, a 25% decline.

The robbery victimization rate declined 27% from 2024 to 2025, while the rate of rape and sexual assault victimization fell 11%.
Property crime also falls
U.S. households experienced an estimated 14.9 million property victimizations in 2025, according to the report.

Missouri to pay $150,000 to settle lawsuit over prisoner’s death by suicide
The settlement follows a judge’s decision to throw out the Department of Corrections’ defense for withholding records. An effort to keep the agreement secret was dropped after The Independent objected.
The Missouri Department of Corrections has settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Willa Hynes, mother of Jahi Hynes , who hanged himself the day after he was placed in administrative segregation on April 3, 2021 (Getty Images).
Missouri must pay $150,000 to the mother of a man who committed suicide in a Southeast Missouri prison, a Mississippi County judge ruled Friday.
Jahi Hynes was 27 when died April 4, 2021, at the Southeast Missouri Correctional Center in Charleston. His mother, Willa Hynes, sued the Department of Corrections, three of the agency’s corporate contractors and 15 individuals in 2024 after forcing the release of records about her son’s death from the department.
In the settlement, the department does not admit any liability for Jahi Hynes’ death and Willa Hynes agreed to drop her claims against all the defendants, including the private contractors.
Associate Circuit Judge Blake Pearson approved the settlement in a brief hearing that came 10 months after the previous judge in the case sanctioned the department and threw out its defense for repeatedly violating court orders to produce records
Under the terms of the settlement, Willa Hynes will receive about $80,000 and her attorneys will receive $60,000 plus the expense of litigation.
“She’s had to wait a long time to get here, and had to fight hard to get here,” attorney Steve Groves said. “But we’re glad the case got resolved, so Miss Hynes can finally get some peace.”
The lawsuit alleged that corrections officials and contract medical personnel ignored Jahi Hynes’ mental health needs and disregarded department rules for the safety of people in administrative segregation.
Jahi Hynes was placed in administrative segregation on April 3, 2021, after allowing the food port door in his cell to strike the hand of a corrections officer, causing minor injuries, and blocking the port with his mattress.
The next day, he hanged himself with a bedsheet.
Hynes’ death is one of more than 630 in department custody from 2021 to 2025, according to records compiled by the Missouri Justice Coalition. The department has been reluctant to release records on the deaths, which reached a record of 139 in 2024.
The highest profile case is the death of Othel Moore on Dec. 8, 2023, in the Jefferson City Correctional Center. Three former corrections officers face criminal charges for assault, with two also charged with second degree murder and the third charged with involuntary manslaughter. Charges against two corrections officers were dropped after they were filed in June 2024.
A hearing is scheduled for Monday in Jefferson City to set a trial date for the three charged in Moore’s death.

Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.
The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.
About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed" and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.
"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."
It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.
Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.
What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year.
"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.
Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.
"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."
A 'jarring' narrative
While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.
Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.
The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.

The court on Friday approved the multinational investment bank's request that the high court clarify whether, and under what circumstances, a bankruptcy court can refuse to enforce an arbitration agreement for claims under Section 362(k) of US Bankruptcy Code if a creditor violates the automatic litigation stay protecting bankrupt people and companies.
Goldman Sachs said that because Section 362(k) issues arise frequently in bankruptcy, a circuit split on this issue reflected lower-court confusion about the FAA's intersection with bankruptcy law.
Goldman Sachs lost a bid in the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit to compel arbitration in a suit alleging it violated bankruptcy law by continuing debt collection efforts despite the stay. The majority of the three-judge Fourth Circuit panel found that arbitration inherently conflicts with the core purposes of the bankruptcy code. Judge Robert B. King, in a dissent, found that the debtors' claims belong in arbitration.
The FAA creates a national policy favoring arbitration when parties have agreed to it. But bankruptcy law is designed to provide a collective, centralized resolution of a debtor's financial affairs. Courts are generally divided over the use of a test that considers whether issues are "core" or "non-core" and whether arbitration creates an inherent conflict.
The Supreme Court hasn't tested the tension between the two statutory schemes. The debtors in this lawsuit, two holders of Apple Card accounts issued by Goldman Sachs, argued the Supreme Court shouldn't take the case because its specific facts — involving a Chapter 13 stay — make it an unsuitable fit to properly resolve the broader legal question.
The American Bankers Association filed an amicus brief in support of Goldman Sachs.
Latham & Watkins LLP represents Goldman Sachs. Kellett & Bartholow PLLC and Giles & Lambert PC represent the consumer borrowers.
The case is Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, U.S., No. 25-1408, cert denied/granted

Today, organizations across Illinois are already working with IBM to explore how quantum computing can scale to computationally difficult challenges. ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP | COP Price Prediction) just raised its quarterly dividend 11% to $0.93. Murphy Oil (NYSE:MUR) followed with a Q3 report that beat estimates on higher production. Brent averaged $97.00/bbl during the quarter, which helped both. Retirees must ask which payout holds up once oil cools off.
Permian Efficiency Funds Conoco’s Raise While Murphy’s Capex Eats Its Cash
Conoco’s Lower 48 assets drove the quarter. Permian pump hours rose 15% from 2025, and capex fell 52.99% year over year. Together they pushed free cash flow to $4.039 billion. That cash paid for $2.4 billion in buybacks and $1 billion in dividends, so the payout took only a small share.

Capex jumped 171.46% after Eagle Ford drilling resumed, which left free cash flow at $48.2 million against $50 million in dividends. That leaves almost no margin for an income stock.
One Lowers Its Breakeven. One Keeps Drilling for the Next Hub.
Conoco is built for durability. Management puts its pre-dividend breakeven in the mid-40s WTI and expects it to approach the low 30s as Willow starts up in early 2029. CFO Connie Haynes-Welsh said, “Buybacks are also how we flex with price.” In practice, repurchases take the hit from oil swings and the dividend stays protected.
Murphy is spending to grow. Lac Da Vang in Vietnam reached first oil on Sept. 27. Management expects Lac Da Vang and Chinook together to generate about $1 billion over five years at $80 Brent. Côte d’Ivoire appraisal could cost another $300 million to $400 million, and CEO Eric Hambly admitted, “I do not know if we will do that.”

Murphy’s 2027 budget, due in late January, is worth watching. Eagle Ford capital is set to rise to around $500 million, and that comes before any Bubale wells. Conoco expects modestly lower 2027 capital, which gives its dividend a calmer track.
Why ConocoPhillips’ Payout Looks Sturdier for Retirement Income
ConocoPhillips shows a stronger dividend profile. Its yield is lower than Murphy’s, but an A-rated balance sheet and net debt at 0.5 times CFO make the payout much stronger. Shortly after the New York City Marathon, tragic news broke: A 24-year-old runner, Rachel Apa, collapsed on the course and died in the hospital after doctors worked for six hours to save her life, according to the New York Times. Apa’s father told NYT the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis (a.k.a. rhabdo).
The news is shocking and saddening—as well as unsettling. Questions are popping up from runners on social media as to how something like this could happen to a young woman who was reportedly a former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University and had spent months training for the marathon.
To help answer some of those questions, we talked to doctors to explain what runners need to know about rhabdo, and how to stay safe.
What Is Rhabdo?
First, know that rhabdo is relatively rare and dying from it is even rarer. Approximately 26,000 cases of rhabdomyolysis are reported annually in the United States, and the mortality rate starts at 10 percent but may go up to 50 percent in severe cases.
In short, rhabdo is a breakdown of muscle that in and of itself is not life-threatening. In fact, Derek M. Fine, MD, a nephrologist at Johns Hopkins Medicine, says that if you were to test creatine kinase (a.k.a. CK, a blood marker of muscle breakdown) in marathon runners after the race, “most” of them would show elevated levels of the enzyme.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that multiple CK tests are the only way to accurately identify rhabdo, though. Normal CK is between 20 and 200 U/L, but rhabdo is diagnosed when it reaches five times the upper limit.
“There’s always a little bit of muscle breakdown and the reason is because, at least in [a] marathon, you’re using the muscles so much that at some point they can run out of an energy supply,” Fine says, adding that the mitochondria can't keep up and make enough of what’s called ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which is your primary source of energy.
Why Is It So Dangerous?
Rhabdo becomes dangerous when it becomes more severe. As muscle tissue breaks down, the body can release harmful substances into the bloodstream, including myoglobin, a protein that can damage the kidneys, and excessive amounts of potassium.
As for myoglobin, the protein can get “stuck” in the kidney and cause kidney failure or injury at various levels, Fine says. “It can be quite severe, but that usually takes a little bit of time to manifest,” he explains.
Fine says that high levels of potassium are probably a bigger risk than myoglobin. “When the muscle cells break up, you get a very large release of potassium into the bloodstream and that potassium then can cause cardiac arrhythmias,” he says. This can cause kidney failure (your kidneys are the organ tasked with getting rid of extra potassium) or potentially sudden cardiac arrest.
“Under normal circumstances, if it’s happening slowly and you’ve got decent kidneys, you pee the potassium out and it never gets that high in the blood,” he says. “If there's severe rhabdo and you have a huge amount of muscles breaking down, you can release a ton of potassium and your body can't get rid of it fast enough.”

The shifting political winds surrounding data centers could buffet the entire U.S. economy, reducing investment in artificial intelligence and slowing growth, according to Wall Street analysts.
The historic tide of money pouring into AI, from data centers and frontier models to state-of-the-art chips and networking gear, has boosted business investment and financial markets in recent years. Federal Reserve researchers recently estimated that spending on data centers, power facilities and other AI-related tech equipment accounted for roughly 20% of U.S. gross domestic product over the preceding year.
In 2026, spending by "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — the companies racing to build data centers — is set to double to around $800 billion and is expected to reach $1 trillion in 2027, according to Capital Economics. Although slowing that buildout might well serve the public interest, given the widespread opposition to data centers, crimping that flow of dollars will have knock-on economic effects.
"Our economy is leveraged on this idea that AI will make us rich," economist Allison Schrager with the Manhattan Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, told CBS News. "There are risks to making it slower — it will mean slower growth."
"Detrimental effects"
Economists and investors now expect the Democrats' sweeping midterm election wins to both slow and increase the cost of data center development across the U.S. By contrast, those victories are unlikely to completely turn off the spigot, experts said, noting that political opposition to data centers isn't uniform, ranging from support for moratoriums on construction to more moderate proposals.
As a result, investment in data centers is likely to continue in the near term, both for projects currently underway and for facilities that have received permits.
For companies investing in AI, the bigger issue will be continuing such capital expenditures at the same pace even as the productivity gains and profits AI is expected to deliver remain largely unrealized for now.
"The high-level calculations essential to justify that level of CapEx, if sustained, we are talking $2 trillion in revenue for major AI companies by the early 2030s, which seems very unlikely," Capital Economics chief North America economist Stephen Brown told CBS News. "Our view is that because of that, there is likely to be some slowdown in data center construction. We are not saying it will stop altogether, but the level of investment is likely to ease. And that would have some detrimental effects on the U.S. economy."
Impact on stocks and consumer spending

The department also projected an end-March cash balance of $1 trillion, a record quarter-end target.
The Treasury's increased cash balance likely reflects greater reliance on short-term bills to finance government spending and deficits. Because bill issuance results in larger and more frequent cash outflows during the month, officials generally seek to maintain a larger buffer. Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.
Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe's management.
Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.
Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, but it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.
The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.
Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn't walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn't stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.
Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.
Crusoe's largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.
